# Essay Prompts

## Prompt 1: Repository Setup and Shared Ownership

> Explain how your group created its CEP repository from the MSDM CEP template, selected an appropriate visibility setting, invited collaborators, and ensured that every member cloned the same repository. Clearly distinguish among using a template, creating a repository, and cloning a repository. Why would independently cloning or copying the original template create problems for group collaboration?

**Principal Author:** Ron Sabilla

To get our group project started, one of us went into the MSDM CEP template on GitHub and clicked "Use this template" to create a brand new repository based on it, which basically copies all the files over without bringing along the original commit history. From there, we set the visibility and the person who created it sent collaborator invites to the rest of the group through the repository settings so everyone had access. Each of us then cloned that same repository to our own laptops using `git clone`, which is what actually connects our local copy to the shared remote on GitHub. It helps to know the difference between these actions — using a template makes a new repo from a blueprint, creating a repo starts one from nothing, and cloning just pulls an existing one down to your computer. If everyone had gone and cloned or copied the original template on their own instead of sharing the one we created, we would have all ended up with completely separate repositories that have no connection to each other. That would have made it impossible to actually collaborate through Git since no one's changes would ever show up for anyone else.

## Prompt 2: Local, Remote, and Working Files

> Explain the relationship among the files on your computer, the local Git repository, and the remote repository on GitHub. In your explanation, distinguish among saving, staging, committing, pushing, fetching, and pulling. Why does saving a QMD file on your computer not make the change available to your teammates?

**Principal Author:** Ron Sabilla

When working with Git, it's important to understand that your files actually exist at three different levels at the same time. There are your working files, which are just the files sitting in your folder that you open and edit; your local Git repository, which is tracking changes on your own computer; and the remote repository on GitHub, which is the shared version everyone on the team syncs to. When you hit save on your `.qmd` file, that only updates the file on your laptop — Git hasn't recorded anything yet. To actually log that change in Git, you have to stage it with `git add` and then commit it with `git commit`, which saves a snapshot of your work to your local repo with a message describing what you did. Even after you commit, your teammates still can't see it until you push it with `git push`, which sends your commits up to GitHub. And on the flip side, when someone else pushes their work, you have to pull it down to your own machine to actually get their updates — which is why just saving your file is nowhere near enough for group collaboration.

## Prompt 3: Document Your Group's Round 1 Workflow

> Describe the order in which group members completed Round 1. For every member, report the member's name, the section or content added, whether the member pulled before editing, the commit message used, and how the member verified that the push succeeded. Present this information in a well-formatted table. Then explain why your group used a sequential workflow for this exercise.

**Principal Author:** Kevin Bachez

During Round 1, our group divided the ten prompts among four members. Brian Vuong completed Prompts 5 through 7, Ron Sabilla completed Prompts 1 and 2, Alexa Bueno completed Prompts 8 through 10, and Kevin Bachez completed Prompts 3 and 4. Based on the GitHub commit history, Brian completed his assigned prompts first, followed by Ron, Alexa, and then Kevin.

| Order | Group Member | Section/Content Added | Pulled Before Editing? | Commit Message | Push Verification Method |
|:-----------|:-----------|:-----------|:-----------|:-----------|:-----------|
| 1 | Brian Vuong | Prompts 5 through 7 | Not confirmed | `address prompts 5 to 7` | Confirmed that the commit and updated sections appeared in the GitHub repository |
| 2 | Ron Sabilla | Prompts 1 and 2 | Not confirmed | `Kevin, Alexa, and Brian, don't forgot to choose what prompts to work on. I did the first two.` | Confirmed that the commit and updated sections appeared in the GitHub repository |
| 3 | Alexa Bueno | Prompts 8 through 10 | Not confirmed | `Address prompt 8 to 10` | Confirmed that the commit and updated sections appeared in the GitHub repository |
| 4 | Kevin Bachez | Prompts 3 and 4 | N/A — cloned the current repository before editing | `Add Kevin's responses for Prompts 3 and 4` | Confirmed that the commit and updated QMD/HTML files appeared in the GitHub repository |

Our group used a sequential workflow to reduce the chance of multiple members editing the same shared QMD file at the same time. By assigning different prompts to each member and having members complete and push their work separately, the group reduced the possibility of overwriting another person's work or creating unnecessary merge conflicts.

The sequential workflow also made the GitHub history easier to follow because each person's contribution could be connected to a specific commit and section of the report. Working from one shared repository gave the group one official version of the project and made it easier to identify the sequence, purpose, and authorship of the changes.

## Prompt 4: A Reliable Everyday CEP Workflow

> Create a numbered checklist that a group member should follow every time they work on the CEP report, beginning before they edit and ending after they push. Explain why pulling before editing and using focused, descriptive commits make collaboration safer and make the project's history more useful.

**Principal Author:** Kevin Bachez

A reliable everyday workflow for working on the CEP report should follow these steps:

1.  **Communicate with the group before beginning** and confirm which section or task you are responsible for.
2.  **Open the shared CEP repository** in Positron or RStudio.
3.  **Pull the most recent version from GitHub before editing** so the local repository contains the newest changes made by the group.
4.  **Review the updated files** and confirm that another group member is not currently editing the same section.
5.  **Edit the section or task assigned to you** and avoid making unnecessary changes to another member's work.
6.  **Save the QMD file** after completing your edits.
7.  **Render the Quarto document** and make sure the HTML report is created without errors.
8.  **Review the rendered report** to confirm that the content and formatting appear correctly.
9.  **Review the changes in the Source Control or Git pane** to see which files were modified.
10. **Stage the appropriate files** that should be included in the commit.
11. **Write a focused and descriptive commit message** that clearly explains the work completed.
12. **Commit the changes** to the local Git repository.
13. **Push the commit to the shared GitHub repository** using Positron, RStudio, or the IDE Terminal.
14. **Verify the push on GitHub** by confirming that the new commit and updated files appear in the remote repository.
15. **Notify the group that the push is complete** so the next member knows it is safe to pull the newest version and begin working.

Pulling before editing is important because another group member may have pushed changes since the last time the repository was opened. If someone begins editing an outdated version of the report, their changes may conflict with newer work already stored on GitHub. Pulling first helps keep the local repository synchronized with the remote repository and reduces the possibility of unnecessary merge conflicts.

Focused and descriptive commit messages also make collaboration safer and the project's history more useful. A message such as `Add Kevin's responses for Prompts 3 and 4` clearly identifies what was completed, while a vague message such as `update` does not provide enough information. Clear commit messages make it easier for the group and instructor to understand the sequence of work, identify who made each contribution, and review previous changes if a problem occurs. Following the pull, edit, render, review, stage, commit, and push workflow helps the group maintain one organized and reliable version of the CEP report.

## Prompt 5: Coordinating Work and Preventing Merge Conflicts (Brian)

> Explain what may happen when two people edit the same lines of the same QMD file and then attempt to push their work. Describe at least three practices your group will use during the CEP to reduce merge conflicts. Include how your group will divide sections, communicate who is editing, and decide when work is ready for another member.

When two collaborators edit the exact same lines of a QMD file simultaneously, Git cannot automatically determine which version to keep. The first person to push their changes to the remote repository will succeed. However, when the second person attempts to push, Git will reject the action to prevent overwriting the first person's work. The second person must then pull the recent changes, which triggers a "merge conflict." The file will be populated with conflict markers (showing both versions), and the second person must manually resolve the discrepancies before they can successfully complete their commit and push.

To minimize these disruptions, our group will implement three primary practices.

::: panel-tabset
### 1. Section Division

We will assign specific sections or distinct files to individual members. By ensuring we are not working on the exact same lines of code or text at the same time, Git can usually auto-merge our files cleanly.

### 2. Active Communication

We will maintain a group chat (e.g., Discord or Slack) where members must announce when they are opening the document to make edits and when they have successfully pushed their work. This "checkout" system prevents overlapping work sessions.

### 3. Frequent Commits

We will make small, frequent commits and push our work regularly. Shorter work cycles mean fewer overarching changes at once, making it much easier to integrate work and limiting the scope of any conflicts that do occur.
:::

## Prompt 6: Responding to a Push Rejection or Merge Conflict (Brian)

> Consider this situation: A group member edits the report without pulling first. Meanwhile, another member pushes changes to the same section. Git rejects the first member's push, and a merge conflict appears after pulling. Explain, in order, what the first member should do... Also explain why force-pushing, deleting a teammate's work, or replacing the repository with an older local copy would be inappropriate.

When a push is rejected due to upstream changes, the first member must immediately pull from the remote repository. This action will trigger a merge conflict notification. The member should then open the affected QMD file in Positron's Merge Editor[^1] or look for standard Git conflict markers (`<<<<<<< HEAD`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`). These markers visually separate the local changes from the incoming changes. The member must carefully compare the two versions, edit the text to keep the desired content (which may be a combination of both), and completely delete all conflict markers. Finally, they must render the document to ensure the formatting is unbroken, save the file, stage it, commit the resolved merge, and push it to GitHub.

[^1]: Positron is an IDE built for data science that includes intuitive visual tools for identifying and resolving Git merge conflicts.

It is absolutely critical to handle conflicts through this established resolution process rather than resorting to destructive alternatives. Force-pushing (`git push --force`) overwrites the remote repository with the local version, permanently erasing the teammate's hard work. Similarly, deleting a teammate's additions to force a commit ignores collaborative progress, and replacing the repository with an older local copy completely corrupts the shared version history. These actions break the fundamental purpose of version control and can set a project back by hours or days.

## Prompt 7: Branches, Issues, and Pull Requests (Brian)

> Based on the collaboration video, explain the purposes of a GitHub Issue, a branch, and a pull request. How could these tools support task assignment, review, and approval during a longer CEP project? Contrast this approach with making a small, coordinated change directly on the main branch. Identify at least one situation in which your group should prefer a branch and pull request.

In a structured GitHub workflow, an **Issue** acts as a tracking ticket for a specific bug, task, or feature, allowing the team to assign responsibilities and discuss requirements before coding begins. A **branch** provides a safe, isolated workspace where a team member can develop a feature without affecting the stable `main` codebase. Once the work on the branch is complete, a **Pull Request (PR)** is opened. A PR is a formal request to merge the branch into `main`, providing a dedicated space for teammates to review the code, suggest edits, and ensure the project renders correctly before final approval. For a long-term CEP project, these tools create a clear audit trail of who is doing what, ensure quality control through peer review, and prevent unstable code from breaking the final report.

This structured approach contrasts heavily with committing directly to the `main` branch. Direct commits are highly efficient for small, coordinated updates—like fixing a quick typo or adding a simple, pre-discussed paragraph where the risk of breaking the project is virtually zero. However, our group should definitively prefer a branch and PR workflow when executing a major structural change, such as overhauling the data analysis pipeline or applying a complex custom CSS theme. In these high-risk scenarios, the isolated branch allows for trial and error, and the PR ensures at least one other set of eyes verifies that the data and formatting are correct before it impacts everyone else's work.

## Prompt 8: Review the Repository History

**Principal Author:** Alexa Bueno

Looking at our repository's commit history, you can see entries tied to different usernames, \@rsabilla, \@brianvuong1, \@kbachez, and \@buenoalexa11, rather than one person uploading a finished file. That alone shows the report was actually built through Git instead of being assembled outside of it and dropped in. The sequence also makes sense chronologically: early commits set up the folder and file structure, then each member's Round 1 commit adds their assigned content ("address prompt 5 to 7," "Address prompt 8 to 10," "address prompt 3 and 4"), and Round 2 commits show people going back through the report to review and add to it, like Brian's "added member commit record." That progression, content getting added first and then refined later, is exactly what you'd expect from a two-round collaboration process, and it wouldn't show up at all if we had just emailed a Word doc back and forth. The most effective commit message in our history is "address prompt 5 to 7," because it tells you precisely what content was added without needing to open the file to check. That's a clear contrast to some of the shorter messages elsewhere in our log, like "edit" or "edits," which don't tell a future reader anything about what actually changed. A specific message like that one is what makes the project history useful later, since you can find exactly when a section was written just by scanning the log instead of digging through every commit.

## Prompt 9: Security, Confidentiality, and Repository Hygiene

**Principal Author:** Alexa Bueno

There are certain things that should never end up in the CEP repository no matter what, even though it's currently private. This includes any real client data, especially anything that could identify a specific company or person, since the assignment instructions specifically told us to use a fake name for our client rather than the real one. It also includes personally identifiable information about survey respondents, passwords, API keys, and access tokens like the ones we'd use to connect to GA4 or BigQuery. These are the kind of things that if accidentally pushed, stay in the commit history forever even if you delete the file afterward, since Git keeps a record of every version. This is where a .gitignore file matters, because it tells Git which files or file types to automatically ignore so they never get staged in the first place, things like local environment files, temporary render files, or anything with credentials in the name. If someone on our team is ever unsure whether something is okay to push, the safest move is to just ask the rest of the group or the professor before committing it, rather than pushing first and hoping it's fine. Once something is on GitHub, especially if the repo gets made public later for the Pages site to work, there's no guarantee it can be fully removed.

## Prompt 10: Group Collaboration Agreement

> All members of this group have reviewed this agreement and agree to follow it for the remainder of the CEP.

**Principal Author:** Alexa Bueno

::: {.callout-note title="Group Collaboration Agreement"}
-   **Pulling and pushing:** Everyone pulls before starting any edit session and pushes as soon as a section is finished, not at the end of the day.
-   **Task assignment:** Sections are assigned in our group chat before anyone starts editing, so two people aren't working on the same part without knowing it.
-   **Simultaneous editing:** We do not edit the same file at the same time. Whoever is working on a section says so in the chat, and says again once they've pushed.
-   **Commit messages:** Messages describe what was actually changed, written in plain language (for example "Add Prompt 9 response" instead of "update").
-   **Branches and pull requests:** We'll use a branch and pull request for anything that touches the structure of the whole report, like a big formatting change or something that could break the render for everyone. Small, coordinated edits to one section can go straight to main.
-   **Conflict resolution:** If a push gets rejected or a conflict pops up, the person who hit it pulls, resolves the conflict markers in Positron, checks with the other person if it's unclear what to keep, and renders before pushing again.
-   **Render verification:** Whoever makes a commit is responsible for confirming the report renders cleanly on their end before pushing.
-   **Confidentiality:** No real client names, credentials, or personal data go into the repository. We use a placeholder name for the client throughout
:::
